lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Boston, July 1920. A line of people stretches down the block.
lines.shot_hint: 1920 street, medium shot travelling along the queue to SECURITIES EXCHANGE CO.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Clerks. Factory workers. Housemaids. All holding cash.
lines.shot_hint: close shots of hands holding bills in the queue

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: They've been promised fifty percent profit in forty-five days.
lines.shot_hint: text card + tear-off calendar 45 DAYS

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: The man taking their money has a prison record. Nobody in that line knows it.
lines.shot_hint: Ponzi at his office window smiling down at the line

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Soon his name will become the word for this scam. And the same trick is still hunting your money today.
lines.shot_hint: push-in on Ponzi, then phone glow

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: So how did one small man in a straw hat fool an entire city?
lines.shot_hint: Ponzi tips his boater

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Charles Ponzi stepped off a ship in Boston in 1903.
lines.shot_hint: night harbor/street, Ponzi with a suitcase

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: By his own account, he had two dollars and fifty cents left.
lines.shot_hint: counter $2.50 over his open hand

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: He drifted from job to job. Then north, to Canada. And into a prison cell, for forgery.
lines.shot_hint: stamp FORGERY on a document, cell bars slide in

lines.speaker: GUARD
lines.text: Name?
lines.shot_hint: close-up guard

lines.speaker: PONZI
lines.text: Remember it. One day you'll read about me.
lines.shot_hint: close-up Ponzi behind bars, grinning

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Remember that cell. Later, a newspaper will find it.
lines.shot_hint: cell door closes

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: By 1919, he was back in Boston. Charming. Broke. And about to open a very lucky letter.
lines.shot_hint: office, envelope on the desk

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Inside was a little slip of paper. An international reply coupon.
lines.shot_hint: hands open the envelope; coupon slides out (framed style)

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Created in 1906, it let you prepay someone's reply postage, anywhere in the world.
lines.shot_hint: map: coupon travels with a dotted route

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: But after the war, money in Europe lost value. The coupon's price didn't change.
lines.shot_hint: line chart: lira falls (orange arrow)

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: So buy coupons cheap in Italy. Trade them in America for more stamps.
lines.shot_hint: framed: EUROPE -> UNITED STATES, big coupon card

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: On paper, it was legal. Here's the catch: you can't pay rent with stamps.
lines.shot_hint: pile of stamps vs a rent bill

lines.speaker: INVESTOR
lines.text: So how do stamps turn into cash?
lines.shot_hint: close-up investor

lines.speaker: PONZI
lines.text: That, my friend, is my secret.
lines.shot_hint: close-up Ponzi, taps his nose

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: He never explained it. People invested anyway.
lines.shot_hint: cash slammed onto his desk by a hand

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: January 1920. The Securities Exchange Company opens its doors.
lines.shot_hint: office sign, Ponzi behind desk

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: The first investors really did get paid. With money from the next investors.
lines.shot_hint: pyramid diagram: new money at the bottom pays the top

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Then those, with the money from the next. It only works while the line keeps growing.
lines.shot_hint: pyramid grows, gets wobbly

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: By the end of July, nearly ten million dollars had poured in.
lines.shot_hint: counter + falling money in the office

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: He bought a mansion. And a big stake in a Boston bank.
lines.shot_hint: mansion + bank stamp OWNER

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Then the crowd got nervous. And came back for their money.
lines.shot_hint: queue turns into a crowd at his door

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Ponzi paid them, smiling. But what nobody knew was who would sink him.
lines.shot_hint: Ponzi hands out cash at the door

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Not the police. His own publicist.
lines.shot_hint: text card, music drops

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: A man he had hired just ten days earlier.
lines.shot_hint: McMasters walks into Ponzi's office, Ponzi shakes his hand

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: William McMasters was hired to make Ponzi look good. He looked at the books instead.
lines.shot_hint: McMasters flips ledger pages

lines.speaker: MCMASTERS
lines.text: He's not rich. He's two million dollars in the hole.
lines.shot_hint: newsroom, McMasters to the editor

lines.speaker: EDITOR
lines.text: Then put it on the front page.
lines.shot_hint: editor slams a fist on the desk

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: On August 2nd, the Boston Post called Ponzi hopelessly insolvent.
lines.shot_hint: newspaper spins in: HOPELESSLY INSOLVENT

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: The math was brutal. His plan needed 160 million coupons. About 27,000 existed.
lines.shot_hint: text card

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Then the paper found that old prison cell in Canada.
lines.shot_hint: newspaper photo of the cell, gold circle

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Within days, Ponzi was arrested. His bank failed. Other banks went down with it.
lines.shot_hint: handcuffs close; bank sign stamp CLOSED

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Investors lost an estimated twenty million dollars. Many got back less than thirty cents on the dollar.
lines.shot_hint: orange counter, coins falling

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Ponzi pleaded guilty to mail fraud. The newspaper won a Pulitzer. He won five years.
lines.shot_hint: stamp GUILTY, stamp PULITZER PRIZE

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: He was deported to Italy, and died in 1949 in a charity ward in Rio. He left seventy-five dollars.
lines.shot_hint: polaroid of Ponzi, counter $75

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: That was his ending. Here's where this reaches your money.
lines.shot_hint: day living room, saver on her phone

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: In 2009, Bernie Madoff pleaded guilty to the biggest Ponzi scheme in history. His statements showed investors about sixty-five billion dollars. Most of it never existed.
lines.shot_hint: statement paper, stamp FAKE

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: And in 2024 alone, Americans told the FBI they lost over six and a half billion dollars to investment fraud.
lines.shot_hint: orange counter over the day lesson set

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: The costume changes. Crypto apps. Trading groups. A friend's can't-lose fund. The trick doesn't.
lines.shot_hint: phone screens pop in

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: The SEC's red flags. Guaranteed high returns with little risk. Returns that never go down. A secret strategy nobody can explain. A seller who isn't registered. Trouble getting your money out.
lines.shot_hint: RED FLAGS board: five flags pop in one by one

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Before you invest a dollar, look them up at investor dot gov.
lines.shot_hint: sticky note slammed on the board: CHECK INVESTOR.GOV

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: A century later, the line is still there. It just moved onto your phone.
lines.shot_hint: callback: the queue, now holding glowing phones

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Fifty percent in forty-five days. Would you have stood in that line?
lines.shot_hint: final question card, music resolves, outro + end screen
